action_criteria.expected_evidence: Five Rascovsky features from her husband's history (disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, stereotyped and compulsive behaviour, executive-predominant profile) with functional decline
action_criteria.label: Structured informant history and bedside cognitive screen scored against the Rascovsky features
action_criteria.rationale: The diagnosis of bvFTD rests on the behavioural features obtained from an informant; the screen documents the cognitive profile.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Executive and social-cognition deficits with a retrieval pattern of memory loss, normal recognition and preserved visuospatial perception
action_criteria.label: Neuropsychological battery including executive and social-cognition measures
action_criteria.rationale: Quantifies the executive and social-cognition profile and whether memory loss is a retrieval deficit or an amnestic storage deficit, which separates bvFTD from Alzheimer disease.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No reversible cause; hyperglycaemia with HbA1c 8.2% and normal TSH on levothyroxine
action_criteria.label: Reversible-cause blood tests: CBC, CMP, TSH, B12, folate, ESR, CRP
action_criteria.rationale: Excludes metabolic, endocrine, nutritional and inflammatory contributors before attributing decline to neurodegeneration; also documents diabetic control and thyroid replacement.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Moderate bifrontal atrophy with posterior sparing, Fazekas 2 white matter disease without infarcts, borderline left hippocampal volume
action_criteria.label: MRI brain without contrast, dementia protocol
action_criteria.rationale: Shows the frontal and anterior temporal atrophy pattern, grades the small-vessel disease and excludes infarcts and hydrocephalus.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Severe frontal and moderate anterior temporal hypometabolism or hypoperfusion with normal posterior cingulate and parietal cortex
action_criteria.label: FDG-PET when the structural picture is unresolved
action_criteria.rationale: With small-vessel disease and a borderline hippocampus, frontal and anterior temporal hypometabolism with posterior sparing supports FTD over AD; perfusion SPECT is the substitute.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Negative amyloid PET, or normal CSF Abeta42/40 ratio and p-tau181
action_criteria.label: AD biomarker (amyloid PET or CSF Abeta42/p-tau) when AD remains in the differential
action_criteria.rationale: A mother with Alzheimer disease, one APOE e4 allele and a borderline left hippocampus keep AD possible; a negative study makes Alzheimer pathology unlikely but does not exclude FTLD.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Identifies or excludes a pathogenic C9orf72, GRN or MAPT variant relevant to prognosis and to relatives
action_criteria.label: Genetic counselling and FTD gene panel (C9orf72, GRN, MAPT)
action_criteria.rationale: Onset about 61 without a suggestive family history: the FTD consortium advises C9orf72 screening in possible or probable bvFTD, UK eligibility does not, so a counselled panel is optional.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General criteria and biomarker evidence only
action_criteria.label: Literature on FTD versus AD and vascular contributors
action_criteria.rationale: General evidence on the criteria and on AD biomarkers; not a clinical step.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not start a cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine): no benefit in FTD, NICE NG97 advises against it, and it may worsen behaviour.
Do not start memantine: a randomised trial showed no benefit in FTD and NICE NG97 advises against it.
Avoid antipsychotics as first-line behavioral therapy given increased cerebrovascular and mortality risk in dementia; reserve for refractory dangerous agitation with specialist oversight.
Avoid benzodiazepines for behavioral control: risk of paradoxical disinhibition and falls.
required_recommendations: Apply the Rascovsky 2011 criteria: state which features are present, the functional decline, and the level of certainty (possible or probable).

Explain why Alzheimer disease (mother with AD, one APOE e4 allele, borderline left hippocampus) and small-vessel disease (Fazekas 2) do not account for the progressive behavioural syndrome, and state that the small-vessel disease coexists.

Treat the vascular risk factors: an individualised HbA1c target of about 7-8% given her cognitive impairment, without hypoglycaemia-prone agents; blood pressure below 130/80 mmHg; and a statin, which is indicated in diabetes at her age.
Address safety and capacity: driving, finances (repeated unrecalled purchases), supervision of her medicines, and any remaining legal or fiduciary roles.
Arrange caregiver education and support for her husband, and a plan for behavioural symptoms that avoids cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine.

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG is non-specific in FTD; not part of the standard dementia workup unless seizures or rapidly progressive course suggest CJD or autoimmune encephalitis.
ECG has no role in the cognitive workup of suspected FTD; reserved for syncope, palpitations, or pre-procedure clearance.
Echocardiography is unrelated to a neurodegenerative cognitive syndrome and adds cost without diagnostic value.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is unrelated to FTD and not indicated absent syncope or palpitations.
Non-contrast head CT lacks the resolution and lobar specificity needed to characterise frontotemporal atrophy; MRI is the standard structural study.
MR spectroscopy has no established role in the routine FTD diagnostic pathway.
Perfusion MRI is not indicated in the standard FTD workup once a structural MRI and FDG-PET (or amyloid PET) have characterised the lobar pattern.
Carotid duplex is a vascular study with no diagnostic role in primary neurodegenerative dementia; small-vessel white matter disease without infarcts or TIA does not call for it.
DaTscan evaluates presynaptic dopaminergic terminals; it is not indicated unless overt parkinsonism raises concern for PD, DLB, or atypical parkinsonism (PSP/CBS overlap).

accepted: Behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD), probable, with concurrent small-vessel cerebrovascular disease

differential.key_features: For: mother with AD, one APOE e4 allele, borderline left hippocampal volume, unrecalled purchases. Against: behavioural onset, recall recovered with cues, normal recognition, frontal atrophy with preserved parietal and posterior cingulate cortex; an amyloid or CSF study settles it if obtained.

differential.diagnosis: Subcortical vascular cognitive impairment as the sole cause
differential.key_features: For: diabetes, hypertension, Fazekas 2. Against: no infarcts or microbleeds, early disinhibition and loss of empathy rather than slowing, lobar frontal atrophy. Small-vessel disease coexists.
Possible at 63 with APOE e4; a negative AD biomarker, if obtained, makes it unlikely.
Against: normal gait, no incontinence, ventricles proportionate to the atrophy.

key_clinical_evidence: Five Rascovsky features (disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, stereotyped and compulsive behaviour, executive-predominant profile) with loss of her judicial role and moderate bifrontal atrophy meet probable bvFTD.
Fazekas 2 small-vessel disease without infarcts coexists but does not explain lobar frontal atrophy and an early social and behavioural syndrome.
The frontal and anterior temporal pattern with relative posterior sparing makes Alzheimer disease less likely; an amyloid or CSF AD biomarker study is optional if doubt remains.
If obtained, a negative amyloid study makes Alzheimer pathology unlikely; it does not exclude FTLD. An APOE e4 allele raises risk but does not diagnose Alzheimer disease.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A mother with late-onset AD does not determine the cause; the behavioural phenotype and the frontal pattern with posterior sparing point to bvFTD, and an AD biomarker settles residual doubt.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchors on familial AD as the explanation.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: APOE e4 is a risk allele, not a diagnostic test; it does not establish Alzheimer disease.
red_herrings.data_point: Direct-to-consumer test reporting one APOE e4 allele
red_herrings.intended_effect: Could be read as evidence of Alzheimer disease.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Moderate small-vessel disease without infarcts does not explain an early behavioural syndrome with lobar frontal atrophy; it coexists and its risk factors need treatment.
red_herrings.data_point: Fazekas 2 white matter hyperintensities in a patient with diabetes and hypertension
red_herrings.intended_effect: Could lead to a diagnosis of vascular cognitive impairment.

bvFTD with vascular comorbidity and AD b.summary: Rascovsky and colleagues (2011) define possible behavioural variant FTD by three of six behavioural and cognitive features, probable bvFTD by added functional decline and frontal or anterior temporal involvement on structural or functional imaging, and definite bvFTD by histopathology or a pathogenic mutation. FDG-PET with frontal and anterior temporal hypometabolism and posterior cingulate sparing favours FTD; amyloid PET or CSF AD markers help when Alzheimer disease remains possible. Treatment is supportive: SSRIs or trazodone for behaviour, caregiver support and safety planning; cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine are not recommended.

metadata.notes: Diagnostic puzzle: probable bvFTD with coexisting small-vessel disease in a 63-year-old retired judge whose mother has Alzheimer disease and who carries one APOE e4 allele. Teaching: APOE e4 does not diagnose AD; a frontal pattern with posterior sparing and retrieval-type memory loss favour bvFTD; an optional amyloid or CSF study makes Alzheimer pathology unlikely if negative but does not exclude FTLD; Fazekas 2 small-vessel disease coexists and its risk factors are treated.

patient.history_present_illness: The Honorable Judge W is a 63-year-old retired judge who presents with her husband of 36 years. The referral comes from the occupational health physician of the judicial system, who describes a 28-month history of progressive behavioral and professional decline that led to a confidential judicial performance review and ultimately to her retirement 18 months ago. Her husband is the primary historian as she dismisses all concerns with judicial formality, stating she 'retired on her own terms' and 'has no medical problems worth discussing.' Her husband reports that the behavioral changes began approximately 28 months ago, initially attributed to the stress of a high-profile murder case. She began making errors in legal proceedings that were out of character — contradicting written rulings made minutes earlier, making statements to litigants that her colleagues found highly inappropriate, and once dismissing a case for a reason that had no legal basis. Outside the courtroom, she began purchasing identical items online without recollection — 14 dresses, 22 identical coffee mugs, and several expensive collectibles she had no prior interest in. She made sexually suggestive comments to a church elder in front of congregation members, causing a significant incident. She has developed a fixed daily routine and becomes highly distressed when any element is altered. She repeats the same three stories at dinner parties, word for word, without awareness of repetition. She has lost interest in her family's activities and shows no emotional engagement with her grandchildren whom she previously adored. Her mother has Alzheimer's disease (diagnosed at age 72 — currently in memory care). Her brother has uncharacterized memory complaints. A direct-to-consumer genetic test she ordered 3 years ago reported one APOE e4 allele. She has type 2 diabetes, hypertension and well-controlled hypothyroidism, and has never taken a statin. There has been no change in gait, no falls and no urinary incontinence.
